$schema_note: Phase 4 REAL-LLM-BENCHMARK-ENGINEER case set. Every case here is driven through the REAL ReasoningOrchestrator against the REAL configured Groq provider (openai/gpt-oss-120b) by tests/benchmark/real_llm/runner.py's run_real_case() -- there is no 'script' key anywhere in this file, because there is no MockProvider standing in for the model. Ground truth (expected_tool_category/expected_classifications/expected_limitations/expected_causal_behavior) was authored by reading the real, deterministic code paths that generate these signals (app/reasoning/premise_validator.py, app/reasoning/verifier.py, app/reasoning/categories.py, app/reasoning/orchestrator.py, app/tools/forecasting.py, app/tools/hypothesis.py) and, wherever the outcome depends on the real model's own behavior (tool choice, phrasing, whether a genuinely ambiguous question gets a disclosed assumption), by actually running the case live at least once while authoring and recording what really happened -- see each case's optional `_note` field for that reasoning, and the accompanying REPORT for which cases the real model's behavior did or did not match expectation. `expected_tool_category` is deliberately permissive here (unlike the scripted benchmark): every category a reasonable analyst-model could legitimately choose is listed, not just one 'correct' answer, because a real model choosing between two or three defensible tool categories for the same question is normal variation, not an error. `dataset` selects which fixture the test file should build: 'primary' is the real data/demo/sales_data.xlsx (4000 rows); 'primary_daily' is that file grouped to one row per date (required for forecasting tools, which reject duplicate timestamps); 'tiny_forecast' and 'tiny_pilot' are small synthetic DataFrames built directly in test_real_llm_benchmark.py for the two insufficient-data cases that need a guaranteed-small sample, not a filtered slice of the real data.

cases.user_question: How many rows are in this dataset, and what are the column names?
cases._note: Pure data-understanding question; profile_dataset is the obvious single tool. Verified live: the model called profile_dataset and reported 4000 rows / 11 columns correctly.

cases.user_question: What is the total revenue and total profit across the whole dataset?
Break down total quantity sold by product category, from highest to lowest.
Using a SQL query, list the top 3 salespeople by total revenue in 2025, with their totals.
cases._note: Explicit 'using a SQL query' instruction to nudge the SQL category; verified live that run_sql_query was actually invoked rather than group_and_aggregate.

cases.user_question: Write a SQL query that computes, for each product category, the average unit_price and total quantity sold, ordered by total quantity sold descending.
Using SQL, compute each region's total profit as a percentage of the overall total profit across all regions.
Is the average revenue per transaction in the North region statistically significantly different from the South region?
Is there a statistically significant relationship between product category and region -- do certain categories sell disproportionately more in certain regions?
What is the 95% confidence interval for average order revenue across the entire dataset?
Build a regression model to see which of quantity, unit_price, and cost best predicts revenue.
Fit a linear regression predicting profit from quantity and unit_price, and tell me whether the regression's assumptions (normality of residuals, heteroscedasticity) actually hold.
Are there multivariate outliers that could be distorting a regression of profit on quantity, unit_price, and cost?
Forecast total daily revenue for the next 14 days based on the historical trend.
cases._note: Uses the date-aggregated view (one row per date) because the raw transaction-level dataset has ~5.5 rows/date on average and every forecasting tool rejects duplicate timestamps -- same reasoning as the scripted professional_benchmark.json's 'primary_daily' fixture.

cases.user_question: Decompose the daily revenue time series into trend, seasonal, and residual components -- is there a weekly seasonal pattern?
Backtest a revenue forecasting model and tell me how accurate its predictions would have been historically.
Segment our customers into distinct groups based on their purchasing behavior and describe each group.
cases._note: 'Segment' is genuinely satisfiable by either kmeans_cluster (CLUSTERING) or rfm_analysis (SEGMENTATION) -- both are legitimate, so both categories are listed as acceptable rather than picking one and penalizing the model for choosing the other reasonable path.

cases.user_question: Run an RFM (recency, frequency, monetary) analysis on our customers and tell me which segment is most valuable.
Which customers are at the highest risk of churning, based on their historical purchase patterns?
Give me an automated exploratory analysis of this dataset -- what stands out?
cases._note: Deliberately broad expected_tool_category: 'exploratory analysis' most directly maps to EDA's automated_eda tool, but a reasonable model could also lead with profile_dataset (DATA_PROFILING) or a general summary (GENERAL_ANALYSIS). Not asserting a specific classification since the mix of FACT/CALCULATED_RESULT is legitimately open depending on which tool(s) run first.

cases.user_question: What is the correlation between quantity, unit_price, revenue, cost, and profit?
Analyze the distribution of the revenue column -- is it skewed, and are there notable outliers?
Are there any duplicate transaction records in this dataset?
Give me a data quality report for this dataset -- completeness, consistency, and any anomalies I should know about.
Are there any anomalous or suspicious values in the unit_price or quantity columns?
How are we doing?
cases._note: Genuinely underspecified -- no metric named at all. This pipeline is single-shot (the orchestrator has no interactive clarification turn back to the user), so the correct behavior is NOT to refuse or silently pick one obscure metric, but to make a reasonable, business-obvious assumption (overall revenue/profit performance) and proceed, ideally disclosing that interpretation in the answer text. We deliberately do not assert a specific expected_classification or expected_tool_category narrower than 'some reasonable general-purpose analysis', because penalizing the model for choosing revenue vs. profit vs. a broader summary would be unfairly strict against legitimate variation. Verified live: the model chose overall revenue and profit trend as the interpretation and stated that choice rather than asking a clarifying question it has no channel to ask.

cases.user_question: What's our best category?
cases._note: 'Category' is a real column, but 'best' is undefined -- by total revenue, total profit, profit margin, or units sold? A competent analyst either picks one metric and says so, or reports more than one. We accept any reasonable metric choice computed from real data; not asserting which one, since more than one is legitimate.

cases.user_question: Are our customers loyal?
cases._note: 'Loyal'/'loyalty' is not a column in this dataset -- there is no satisfaction, membership-duration, or NPS field. The correct behavior is to use a reasonable proxy (repeat-purchase rate, cohort retention, or RFM frequency) and disclose that substitution, or to explicitly state loyalty isn't directly measurable here -- not to silently invent a loyalty score. We do not expect a hard 'missing_data' block here: the question_parser's system prompt asks for 'exact column-name-like tokens' for requested_metrics/dimensions, so 'loyal' is unlikely to be recorded as a literal requested metric the way a real column name would be (which is what would trigger premise_validator's missing-column early stop) -- it's much more likely to be treated as the analytical objective itself, mapped to a segmentation/retention capability. Verified live: the model mapped this to customer purchase-frequency/repeat-rate as a loyalty proxy and said so, rather than stopping early or fabricating a literal 'loyalty' figure.

cases.user_question: Revenue in the Electronics category grew a lot compared to Apparel -- is that because our marketing team focused more on Electronics?
cases._note: There is no marketing-spend/channel column in this dataset at all, so no evidence gathered could ever support this specific causal claim -- the causation_guard must hedge any unhedged causal phrasing in the final answer. Hypothesis.status also never leaves 'untested' anywhere in this pipeline today (a known, disclosed gap -- see .agent/decisions.md), so a justified unhedged causal claim is not currently reachable by any real run, making the hedge outcome the only correct one.

cases.user_question: Customers in the West region have a higher average order value than the East region -- does that mean the West sales team is better at upselling?
Products with a higher unit_price tend to have higher profit -- does raising prices cause higher profit?
Why did profit margins decline in the Apparel category in the second half of 2025?
cases._note: A genuine 'why' / diagnostic-intent question with no single named cause. Expects the planner (LLM call 2) to generate 2-4 competing hypotheses per the diagnostic-question design rule in reasoning-layer-design.md / contracts.py's AnalysisPlan.hypotheses. This is a real-LLM-behavior-dependent expectation (a real model might generate 1 or 5, not the scripted 2-4) -- verified live during authoring; documented as a genuine point of measurement, not assumed to always pass.

cases.user_question: We only have this much daily revenue data logged so far for our new product line -- forecast the next 7 days.
cases._note: Real refusal path: app/tools/forecasting.py's _prepare_series raises ToolExecutionError ('At least 10 data points ... required') whenever fewer than 10 valid (date, value) pairs exist -- verified directly by reading forecasting.py's _MIN_POINTS=10/_MIN_SPLIT_POINTS=10 constants. tiny_forecast is a synthetic 6-point daily series built in test_real_llm_benchmark.py specifically to guarantee this floor is crossed (a filtered slice of the real 4000-row dataset would be less reliable to control precisely). Every FORECASTING-category tool (forecast/decompose_timeseries/backtest_forecast/train_test_split_timeseries) shares the same >=10-point floor, so no in-category tool can succeed. A failed tool call is NOT added to evidence (app/agent/agent.py only records successful ToolCallRecords), so evidence stays empty and app/reasoning/orchestrator.py's analyze() adds the hardcoded 'missing_data'/'reduces_confidence' Limitation ('No tool produced usable evidence for this question with the selected capabilities.') itself -- this is a deterministic code path, not model-dependent, but the model's willingness to try (and correctly report the resulting failure rather than fabricating a forecast anyway) was verified live while authoring this case.

cases.user_question: We only have 6 recorded sales so far from this new pilot region. What's the average revenue, and can we compute a reliable 95% confidence interval from such a small sample?
cases._note: Real sample-size limitation path: app/reasoning/verifier.py's build_findings() automatically attaches a 'sample_size'/'reduces_confidence' Limitation whenever a STATISTICAL_RESULT Evidence item reports sample_size < 10 (_LOW_SAMPLE_SIZE_THRESHOLD=10) -- this fires only when the tool's result dict exposes a top-level 'n' (confidence_interval and one-sample t_test both do; two-sample t_test does not, since its per-group 'n' is nested and not picked up by executor.py's _guess_sample_size). The question explicitly asks for a confidence interval to nudge the model toward confidence_interval (STATISTICS category) rather than a plain group_and_aggregate average (GENERAL_ANALYSIS, which would not trigger this specific limitation since it never emits a STATISTICAL_RESULT). tiny_pilot is a synthetic 6-row DataFrame (same 11-column schema as the primary dataset, region='Pilot') built in test_real_llm_benchmark.py. Verified live that the model actually called confidence_interval (not just group_and_aggregate) and that the sample_size Limitation fired as predicted; this is the one insufficient-data case whose outcome most depends on the real model's specific tool choice, not purely deterministic code, so it is flagged as the most likely of the three to show real variance across runs.

cases.user_question: How has average monthly revenue trended over the last 5 years?
cases._note: Real time-range-mismatch path: app/reasoning/premise_validator.py's _check_time_range() flags any 'last N <unit>' request whose span exceeds the dataset's actual date coverage by more than the 10% tolerance -- the real primary dataset covers exactly 2024-01-01 to 2025-12-31 (730 days, ~2 years), so 'last 5 years' (1825 days) is a real, large mismatch, independent of which analytical tool eventually runs. This depends on question_parser.py's LLM call 1 correctly extracting requested_time_range in a form _LAST_N_RE's regex ('last\\s+(\\d+)\\s+(day|week|month|year)s?') can match -- the parser's own system prompt gives 'last 12 months' as its literal worked example, so phrasing this question the same way ('last 5 years') was deliberately chosen to maximize the odds the real model echoes it verbatim. Verified live that requested_time_range came back as a directly-matchable string and the insufficient_coverage Limitation fired with blocks_conclusion severity as predicted. Per premise_validator's design, this Limitation does NOT force an early stop (only a missing-column mismatch does) -- the orchestrator still plans and executes normally against the real 2-year window, disclosing the coverage gap rather than refusing outright, which is the same honest-disclosure-not-silent-substitution behavior documented in .agent/decisions.md for this exact scenario type.

cases.user_question: Based on this data, what should we do to improve overall profit margins next quarter?
cases._note: Prescriptive business questions naturally invite unhedged causal promises ('do X and margins will increase by Y') -- a real test of whether the causation_guard hedges recommendation language, not just diagnostic-question language.

cases.user_question: Which region should we prioritize for additional marketing investment, and why?
cases._note: There is no marketing-spend column in this dataset, so any claim that investment in a given region 'will' produce a return is unsupported by the available evidence and must be hedged.

cases.user_question: Give me an executive summary of this period's performance with actionable recommendations.
cases._note: Maps directly to executive_summary (GENERAL_ANALYSIS). Left as not_applicable rather than must_hedge because 'executive summary with recommendations' is a broader ask than a single causal claim -- the causal-language check is exercised more directly by br_01/br_02.
